title: Ἡ Ἀσπὶς τελεῖται
about: The second city on the shield is under siege. Two armies lie round it, divided between sacking it and sharing out its wealth, while the besieged secretly arm and march out, led by golden Ares and Athena, to ambush a river where the herds are watered. They kill the shepherds and drive off the animals; the besiegers hear the din, ride out, and a battle is fought on the river-bank, with Strife, Uproar and the Death-spirit among the fighters. Hephaestus then sets on the shield a field being ploughed, a king’s estate where reapers cut and binders bind while a feast is prepared, a vineyard at the vintage with a boy singing to the lyre, a herd of cattle attacked by two lions, a pasture of sheep, and a dancing-ground like the one Daedalus made for Ariadne, with young men and girls dancing and a minstrel and two tumblers in their midst. The river Oceanus runs round the rim. The god adds a breastplate, a helmet and greaves, lays the armour before Thetis, and she carries it down from Olympus like a hawk.

sentences.t:
τὴν δ’ ἑτέρην πόλιν ἀμφὶ δύω στρατοὶ ἥατο λαῶν
τεύχεσι λαμπόμενοι·
sentences.l:
And the other city, about it two armies were sitting of the people,
shining in their armour;
sentences.i: Around the other city sat two armies of men, shining in their armour;
sentences.n: The shield now shows its second city, the one at war, set against the city of the wedding and the lawsuit (18.491–508). τὴν … ἑτέρην ‘the other’ is the second of the two, and ἀμφί ‘about’ takes πόλιν. ἥατο is the epic imperfect of ἧμαι ‘sit’, here ‘lay encamped’; λαῶν ‘of the people’ depends on στρατοί ‘armies’. λαμπόμενοι ‘shining’ (λάμπομαι) goes with τεύχεσι ‘in their armour’.

sentences.t:
δίχα δέ σφισιν ἥνδανε βουλή,
ἠὲ διαπραθέειν ἢ ἄνδιχα πάντα δάσασθαι
κτῆσιν ὅσην πτολίεθρον ἐπήρατον ἐντὸς ἔεργεν·
sentences.i: and their counsel was divided, either to sack it or to share out all the property in two parts, all that the lovely citadel held within;
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 510. δίχα ‘in two ways’ and ἥνδανε ‘was pleasing’ (imperfect of ἁνδάνω, with the dative σφισιν ‘to them’) say that the besiegers were of two minds; the two plans follow as ἠέ … ἤ ‘either … or’. διαπραθέειν is an epic aorist infinitive of διαπέρθω ‘sack utterly’, and ἄνδιχα ‘in two parts’ is ἀνά + δίχα. κτῆσιν ὅσην ‘as much property as’; ἔεργεν = εἶργεν ‘shut in, held’; πτολίεθρον ‘citadel’ is the city itself.

sentences.t: οἳ δ’ οὔ πω πείθοντο, λόχῳ δ’ ὑπεθωρήσσοντο.
sentences.l: But they were not yet obeying, and for an ambush they were arming secretly.
sentences.i: But the besieged would not yet give in, and were arming in secret for an ambush.
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ‘but they’ are the people of the besieged city, as the next lines show. πείθοντο ‘obeyed’ means that they would not yet comply with either plan of the besiegers; the Greek does not say more. λόχῳ is a dative of purpose, ‘for an ambush’. ὑποθωρήσσομαι is ‘arm secretly’ (ὑπο- ‘secretly, in hiding’, θωρήσσω ‘arm’).

sentences.t:
τεῖχος μέν ῥ’ ἄλοχοί τε φίλαι καὶ νήπια τέκνα
ῥύατ’ ἐφεσταότες, μετὰ δ’ ἀνέρες οὓς ἔχε γῆρας·
sentences.l:
The wall, indeed, dear wives and infant children
were guarding, standing upon it, and among them the men whom old age held;
sentences.i: Their dear wives and little children stood on the wall and guarded it, and with them the men whom old age held;
sentences.n: The people left in the city defend it: the women, the children and the old men who stay behind. ῥύατ’ is the third-plural imperfect ῥύατο of ῥύομαι ‘protect, guard’, with τεῖχος ‘the wall’ as object; ἐφεσταότες is the perfect participle of ἐφίστημι, ‘standing upon it’, masculine though it covers wives and children. μετά is an adverb, ‘among them’. οὓς ἔχε γῆρας ‘whom old age held’ means held back from fighting; ἔχε is an unaugmented imperfect. ῥ’ is ῥα.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἴσαν· ἦρχε δ’ ἄρά σφιν Ἄρης καὶ Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη
ἄμφω χρυσείω,
sentences.l:
And they went; and led them Ares and Pallas Athena,
both golden,
sentences.i: The men of the city marched out, with Ares and Pallas Athena leading them, both of them golden,
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ‘and they’ are the besieged, now marching out toward the place of ambush. ἴσαν is the imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’, and ἦρχε ‘led’ has the dative σφιν ‘them’ (‘led for them’). Ares and Athena are the gods figured on the shield, and as figures wrought by Hephaestus they are of gold. ἄμφω χρυσείω is a dual, ‘both golden’, and the duals carry on into the next unit.

sentences.t:
χρύσεια δὲ εἵματα ἕσθην,
καλὼ καὶ μεγάλω σὺν τεύχεσιν, ὥς τε θεώ περ
ἀμφὶς ἀριζήλω·
sentences.i: and the two wore golden clothes, fine and great in their armour, as gods are, plain to see apart from the rest;
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 517. ἕσθην is a dual, ‘the two were wearing’ (ἕννυμι ‘clothe’), and καλώ, μεγάλω, θεώ and ἀριζήλω are duals too. εἵματα ‘clothes’. ἀμφίς means ‘apart, on either side’, and here sets the two gods off from the men; ἀρίζηλος ‘conspicuous’. ὥς τε θεώ περ ‘as gods indeed’ says that they look what they are, and larger than the men, as the next unit adds.

sentences.t: λαοὶ δ’ ὑπολίζονες ἦσαν.
sentences.l: and the people were somewhat smaller.
sentences.i: while the people with them were smaller.
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 519. λαοί ‘the people’ are the ordinary men who follow the two gods. ὑπολίζων is a rare word, understood as ‘rather small, smaller’; its formation is not certain.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ὅτε δή ῥ’ ἵκανον ὅθι σφίσιν εἶκε λοχῆσαι
ἐν ποταμῷ, ὅθι τ’ ἀρδμὸς ἔην πάντεσσι βοτοῖσιν,
ἔνθ’ ἄρα τοί γ’ ἵζοντ’ εἰλυμένοι αἴθοπι χαλκῷ.
sentences.l:
And when they came to where it suited them to lie in ambush,
at a river, where there was a watering-place for all the herds,
there then they sat down, wrapped in fire-faced bronze.
sentences.i: When they came to the place where it suited them to lie in wait, at a river where there was a watering-place for all the herds, they sat down there, wrapped in bronze that has the look of fire.
sentences.n: ὅθι σφίσιν εἶκε λοχῆσαι ‘where it suited them to ambush’: εἶκε is impersonal, ‘it was fitting’, with the infinitive λοχῆσαι. ἀρδμός ‘watering-place’; βοτά are grazing animals, herds and flocks. ἵζοντ’ = ἵζοντο ‘sat down’. εἰλυμένοι is the participle of εἰλύω ‘wrap, cover’, and αἴθοψ ‘fire-faced’ (αἴθω ‘burn’ + ὤψ ‘face’) is the bronze that glows like fire.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δ’ ἔπειτ’ ἀπάνευθε δύω σκοποὶ εἵατο λαῶν
δέγμενοι ὁππότε μῆλα ἰδοίατο καὶ ἕλικας βοῦς.
sentences.l:
And apart from them then two lookouts of the people were sitting,
waiting for when they should see flocks and crumple-horned cattle.
sentences.i: Some way off from them sat two lookouts from the people, waiting for the moment when they should see flocks and crumple-horned cattle.
sentences.n: σκοποί ‘lookouts’ are posted away from the main body. εἵατο is the epic imperfect of ἧμαι ‘sit’. δέγμενοι ‘waiting’ (δέχομαι, ‘waiting for’) takes ὁππότε with the optative ἰδοίατο ‘for the time when they should see’. μῆλα ‘flocks’; ἕλικας βοῦς ‘crumple-horned cattle’, the cattle whose horns curve.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ τάχα προγένοντο, δύω δ’ ἅμ’ ἕποντο νομῆες
τερπόμενοι σύριγξι· δόλον δ’ οὔ τι προνόησαν.
sentences.l:
And these soon came forward, and two herdsmen came along with them,
delighting in reed-pipes; and the trick they did not at all foresee.
sentences.i: The herds soon came forward, and two herdsmen came along with them, delighting in their reed-pipes; they had no thought of the trick.
sentences.n: οἳ δὲ τάχα προγένοντο: ‘they’ must be the cattle and sheep, since the herdsmen are named next as following them. προγένοντο ‘came forward’. νομῆες ‘herdsmen’, and δύω is the numeral ‘two’. σῦριγξ is a reed-pipe, the shepherd’s pipe, here in the dative plural σύριγξι. δόλον δ’ οὔ τι προνόησαν ‘they did not at all foresee the trick’ (προνοέω).

sentences.t:
οἳ μὲν τὰ προϊδόντες ἐπέδραμον, ὦκα δ’ ἔπειτα
τάμνοντ’ ἀμφὶ βοῶν ἀγέλας καὶ πώεα καλὰ
ἀργεννέων οἰῶν, κτεῖνον δ’ ἐπὶ μηλοβοτῆρας.
sentences.l:
These, having seen them beforehand, ran upon them, and quickly then
they cut off all round the herds of cattle and the fine flocks
of white sheep, and killed the shepherds besides.
sentences.i: The ambushers, seeing them ahead, ran out upon them and quickly cut off the herds of cattle and the fine flocks of white sheep, and killed the shepherds too.
sentences.n: οἳ μέν ‘these’ are the men in ambush, answering οἳ δέ, the herds, in 525. τὰ προϊδόντες ‘having seen them ahead of time’; ἐπέδραμον ‘ran upon’. τάμνοντ’ is τάμνοντο, the middle of τέμνω ‘cut’, here ‘cut off’ the animals for themselves, with ἀμφί ‘all round’. ἀγέλη ‘herd’, πῶυ ‘flock’, ἀργεννός ‘white’, οἶς ‘sheep’. μηλοβοτήρ is ‘shepherd’ (μῆλα ‘flocks’ + βόσκω ‘feed’), and ἐπί adds them: ‘besides’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ὡς οὖν ἐπύθοντο πολὺν κέλαδον παρὰ βουσὶν
εἰράων προπάροιθε καθήμενοι, αὐτίκ’ ἐφ’ ἵππων
βάντες ἀερσιπόδων μετεκίαθον, αἶψα δ’ ἵκοντο.
sentences.l:
And they, when they heard much din among the cattle,
sitting before the assembly-places, straightway on horses
mounting, high-stepping, went after them, and quickly came.
sentences.i: But the besiegers, sitting before their meeting-places, heard the great din among the cattle; at once they mounted their high-stepping horses and went after them, and soon arrived.
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ‘but they’ are the besiegers, who had been sitting in debate (510–512). εἰράων is a very rare word whose sense is not known; the guess ‘places of assembly’ suits their council and is used here. κέλαδος ‘din’; ἐπύθοντο ‘heard, learned of’ (πυνθάνομαι). ἐφ’ ἵππων βάντες ‘having mounted horses’; ἀερσίπους ‘high-stepping’, the usual explanation, from ἀείρω ‘lift’ + πούς ‘foot’. μετεκίαθον ‘went after’; ἵκοντο ‘arrived’.

sentences.t:
στησάμενοι δ’ ἐμάχοντο μάχην ποταμοῖο παρ’ ὄχθας,
βάλλον δ’ ἀλλήλους χαλκήρεσιν ἐγχείῃσιν.
sentences.l:
And having taken their stand, they fought a fight beside the banks of the river,
and they hurled at one another with bronze-fitted spears.
sentences.i: They took their stand and fought a battle beside the banks of the river, and hurled bronze-fitted spears at one another.
sentences.n: στησάμενοι δ’ ἐμάχοντο μάχην ‘having taken their stand they fought a fight’ is a formula the Odyssey also has, there ‘beside the swift ships’; here the place is the river-bank (ὄχθας), and ποταμοῖο has the epic ending -οιο. χαλκήρης ‘bronze-fitted’ is said of spears, and ἐγχείη is ‘spear’.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ Ἔρις ἐν δὲ Κυδοιμὸς ὁμίλεον, ἐν δ’ ὀλοὴ Κήρ,
ἄλλον ζωὸν ἔχουσα νεούτατον, ἄλλον ἄουτον,
ἄλλον τεθνηῶτα κατὰ μόθον ἕλκε ποδοῖιν·
sentences.i: Strife and Uproar thronged among them, and baleful Death-spirit too, holding one man alive and freshly wounded, another unwounded, and dragging a third, who was dead, by the feet through the press of battle;
sentences.n: Ἔρις ‘Strife’, Κυδοιμός ‘Uproar’ and Κήρ ‘Death-spirit’ are powers of battle, personified, and ἐν … ἐν … ἐν ‘among them’ puts them in the crowd. ὁμίλεον ‘kept thronging’ has two subjects, and only Κήρ is the subject of the feminine ἔχουσα ‘holding’ and of ἕλκε ‘was dragging’ (an unaugmented imperfect). ὀλοή ‘baleful’. νεούτατος ‘freshly wounded’ and ἄουτος ‘unwounded’ both come from οὐτάω ‘wound’. μόθος ‘press’ of battle. ποδοῖιν is a dual, ‘by the two feet’.

sentences.t: εἷμα δ’ ἔχ’ ἀμφ’ ὤμοισι δαφοινεὸν αἵματι φωτῶν.
sentences.l: and a garment she had about her shoulders, blood-red with the blood of men.
sentences.i: and the garment about her shoulders was blood-red with the blood of men.
sentences.n: The garment is Κήρ’s own. εἷμα ‘garment’ is singular; ἔχ’ is ἔχε, ‘had’. δαφοινεός ‘blood-red’ is a longer form of δαφοινός, whose exact sense is not certain (δα- ‘very’ + φοινός ‘red’ is the usual guess), and αἵματι ‘with blood’ is a dative of means. φώς ‘man’ has the genitive plural φωτῶν.

sentences.t:
ὡμίλευν δ’ ὥς τε ζωοὶ βροτοὶ ἠδ’ ἐμάχοντο,
νεκρούς τ’ ἀλλήλων ἔρυον κατατεθνηῶτας.
sentences.l:
And they kept thronging like living mortals and fought,
and dragged one another’s corpses, the fallen dead.
sentences.i: They thronged and fought like living men, and dragged away one another’s dead.
sentences.n: The subject is now the figures of the fighters. ὡμίλευν = ὡμίλεον, the same verb as in 535, ‘kept thronging’. ὥς τε ζωοὶ βροτοί ‘like living mortals’ reminds the hearer that these are wrought figures. νεκρούς … κατατεθνηῶτας: κατατεθνηῶτας is the perfect participle of καταθνήσκω ‘be dead’, so ‘corpses, dead ones’. ἔρυον ‘dragged’ (ἐρύω).

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ ἐτίθει νειὸν μαλακὴν πίειραν ἄρουραν
εὐρεῖαν τρίπολον· πολλοὶ δ’ ἀροτῆρες ἐν αὐτῇ
ζεύγεα δινεύοντες ἐλάστρεον ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα.
sentences.l:
And on it he set a fallow field, soft, rich, a plough-land,
wide, thrice-ploughed; and many ploughmen in it
were driving their teams, turning them this way and that.
sentences.i: And on it he set a field of soft, rich fallow, wide plough-land ploughed three times; and many ploughmen on it drove their teams, wheeling them this way and that.
sentences.n: ἐν δ’ ἐτίθει ‘and on it he set’ opens a new scene on the shield, as it does at 550, 561 and 607; the imperfect of τίθημι with ἐν ‘on it’ (the shield). νειός is land ploughed and left fallow, and νειὸν … ἄρουραν are in apposition, with μαλακήν ‘soft’ and πίειραν ‘rich’. τρίπολος ‘ploughed three times’. ἀροτῆρες ‘ploughmen’; ζεύγεα ‘teams’ (yoked pairs); δινεύοντες ‘wheeling them round’; ἐλάστρεον ‘drove’ (ἐλαστρέω, a by-form of ἐλαύνω).

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ὁπότε στρέψαντες ἱκοίατο τέλσον ἀρούρης,
τοῖσι δ’ ἔπειτ’ ἐν χερσὶ δέπας μελιηδέος οἴνου
δόσκεν ἀνὴρ ἐπιών·
sentences.i: Whenever they had turned and reached the field’s boundary, a man would come up to them and put a cup of honey-sweet wine into their hands;
sentences.n: ὁπότε with the optative ἱκοίατο ‘whenever they came’ makes this a repeated event. δόσκεν is the iterative of δίδωμι (the suffix -σκ-, ‘would give’), unaugmented. τοῖσι δ’ ἔπειτα ‘to them then’ is the ploughmen; ἐπιών ‘coming up’. τέλσον is a rare word for the boundary or end of the field.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δὲ στρέψασκον ἀν’ ὄγμους,
ἱέμενοι νειοῖο βαθείης τέλσον ἱκέσθαι.
sentences.l:
and they would turn back along the furrows,
eager to reach the boundary of the deep fallow.
sentences.i: and they would turn again along the furrows, eager to reach the boundary of the deep fallow land.
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 546. τοί is the article as a pronoun, ‘they’, the ploughmen. στρέψασκον is the iterative of στρέφω ‘turn’, ‘would turn’. ὄγμος ‘furrow, row’. ἱέμενοι ‘eager’ (ἵεμαι). βαθείης ‘deep’ agrees with νειοῖο, the genitive of νειός.

sentences.t:
ἣ δὲ μελαίνετ’ ὄπισθεν, ἀρηρομένῃ δὲ ἐῴκει,
χρυσείη περ ἐοῦσα· τὸ δὴ περὶ θαῦμα τέτυκτο.
sentences.l:
And it grew black behind them, and was like land that has been ploughed,
though it was golden; that indeed was wrought a marvel beyond all.
sentences.i: But behind them it grew black, like ploughed land, though it was gold; and that was the great marvel of its making.
sentences.n: ἣ δέ ‘and it’ is the field. μελαίνετο ‘was growing black’; ἀρηρομένῃ is the dative perfect participle of ἀρόω ‘plough’, with ἐῴκει ‘was like’. χρυσείη περ ἐοῦσα ‘though it was golden’ (περ is concessive). τέτυκτο is the pluperfect passive of τεύχω ‘had been made’, and περί is an adverb, ‘beyond all, exceedingly’, with θαῦμα ‘marvel’.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ ἐτίθει τέμενος βασιλήϊον· ἔνθα δ’ ἔριθοι
ἤμων ὀξείας δρεπάνας ἐν χερσὶν ἔχοντες.
sentences.l:
And on it he set a royal precinct; and there hired labourers
were reaping, sharp sickles in their hands holding.
sentences.i: And on it he set a king’s estate; and there hired labourers were reaping, with sharp sickles in their hands.
sentences.n: τέμενος is a plot of land marked off for one owner, here the king’s own estate; the Odyssey uses it of ploughland as well as of a god’s ground. βασιλήϊον ‘of a king, royal’. ἔριθος ‘hired labourer’; ἤμων ‘were reaping’, imperfect of ἀμάω; δρεπάνη ‘sickle’.

sentences.t:
δράγματα δ’ ἄλλα μετ’ ὄγμον ἐπήτριμα πῖπτον ἔραζε,
ἄλλα δ’ ἀμαλλοδετῆρες ἐν ἐλλεδανοῖσι δέοντο.
sentences.l:
Some handfuls along the swath thick-set were falling to the ground,
and others the sheaf-binders with bands were binding.
sentences.i: Some of the cut handfuls fell thick and fast to the ground along the swath, and others the sheaf-binders bound with bands.
sentences.n: δράγματα ‘handfuls’ of cut grain; ἄλλα … ἄλλα ‘some … others’. ὄγμος is the row left by the reapers, here ‘swath’; ἐπήτριμα ‘close together, thick’. ἀμαλλοδετήρ ‘sheaf-binder’ (ἀμάλλη ‘sheaf’ + δέω ‘bind’). ἐλλεδανοί is a rare word, taken as ‘bands’ for tying sheaves, but its sense is not quite certain. δέοντο ‘were binding’ (middle of δέω).

sentences.t:
τρεῖς δ’ ἄρ’ ἀμαλλοδετῆρες ἐφέστασαν· αὐτὰρ ὄπισθε
παῖδες δραγμεύοντες ἐν ἀγκαλίδεσσι φέροντες
ἀσπερχὲς πάρεχον·
sentences.i: Three sheaf-binders stood ready, and behind them boys gathered up the handfuls and, carrying them in their arms, kept supplying them without pause;
sentences.n: ἐφέστασαν ‘stood by, at hand’ (ἐφίστημι, intransitive past). ὄπισθε ‘behind’ the binders, where the boys work. δραγμεύοντες ‘gathering handfuls’ (a rare verb from δράγμα); ἀγκαλίς ‘armful’, ἐν ἀγκαλίδεσσι ‘in their arms’. ἀσπερχές ‘unceasingly’; πάρεχον ‘supplied’ (παρέχω), with the handfuls as the understood object.

sentences.t:
βασιλεὺς δ’ ἐν τοῖσι σιωπῇ
σκῆπτρον ἔχων ἑστήκει ἐπ’ ὄγμου γηθόσυνος κῆρ.
sentences.l:
and the king among them in silence,
holding a sceptre, stood by the swath, glad in heart.
sentences.i: and among them the king stood silent by the swath, holding his sceptre, glad at heart.
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 556. σιωπῇ ‘in silence’ (the king watches without speaking). ἑστήκει is the pluperfect of ἵστημι, with the sense ‘was standing’; ἐπ’ ὄγμου ‘by the swath’. γηθόσυνος κῆρ ‘glad in heart’: κῆρ is an accusative of respect.

sentences.t:
κήρυκες δ’ ἀπάνευθεν ὑπὸ δρυῒ δαῖτα πένοντο,
βοῦν δ’ ἱερεύσαντες μέγαν ἄμφεπον·
sentences.l:
And heralds apart, beneath an oak, were busied with a feast,
and a great ox, having slaughtered it, were busy about;
sentences.i: Apart from them, under an oak, heralds were preparing a feast; they had slaughtered a great ox and were busy about it;
sentences.n: κήρυκες ‘heralds’ are presumably the king’s servants. πένοντο ‘were busied’, with δαῖτα ‘a feast’, means preparing it. δρυΐ is the dative of δρῦς ‘oak’. ἱερεύσαντες ‘having slaughtered’ (ἱερεύω); ἄμφεπον ‘were busy about’ (ἀμφέπω), so the ox is being dressed for the meal.

sentences.t:
αἳ δὲ γυναῖκες
δεῖπνον ἐρίθοισιν λεύκ’ ἄλφιτα πολλὰ πάλυνον.
sentences.l:
and the women, for the labourers’ meal,
white barley-meal, much of it, were sprinkling.
sentences.i: and the women sprinkled white barley-meal thickly for the labourers’ meal.
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 559. αἳ δὲ γυναῖκες: αἱ is the article as a demonstrative, ‘the women’. δεῖπνον ἐρίθοισιν ‘a meal for the labourers’. ἄλφιτα ‘barley-meal’ is a plural; πάλυνον ‘were sprinkling’ (παλύνω).

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ ἐτίθει σταφυλῇσι μέγα βρίθουσαν ἀλωὴν
καλὴν χρυσείην· μέλανες δ’ ἀνὰ βότρυες ἦσαν,
ἑστήκει δὲ κάμαξι διαμπερὲς ἀργυρέῃσιν.
sentences.l:
And on it he set a vineyard heavily laden with grapes,
fine, golden; and black clusters were up on it,
and it stood throughout on poles of silver.
sentences.i: And on it he set a vineyard heavy with grapes, fine and golden; the clusters on it hung black, and all of it stood on silver poles.
sentences.n: ἀλωή is a cultivated plot, elsewhere an orchard or a threshing-floor; the grapes and the vintage make it a vineyard here. σταφυλῇσι ‘with grapes’ (dative of means), μέγα βρίθουσαν ‘heavily laden’ (βρίθω ‘be heavy’). βότρυς ‘cluster’; ἀνά is an adverb, ‘up on it’. κάμαξ ‘vine-pole’; διαμπερές ‘all through, throughout’; ἑστήκει ‘stood’.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δὲ κυανέην κάπετον, περὶ δ’ ἕρκος ἔλασσε
κασσιτέρου·
sentences.l:
And around it a dark ditch, and around that a fence he drove
of tin;
sentences.i: Around it he drew a dark ditch, and around that he ran a fence of tin;
sentences.n: ἀμφί and περί are adverbs, ‘round about’, and one verb, ἔλασσε (aorist of ἐλαύνω ‘drive, drive on’), serves both objects: κάπετον ‘ditch’ and ἕρκος ‘fence’. κυανέη ‘dark’ is a colour word (from κύανος, a dark-blue substance), kept as ‘dark’ as for the brows and the cloud elsewhere. κασσίτερος ‘tin’.

sentences.t:
μία δ’ οἴη ἀταρπιτὸς ἦεν ἐπ’ αὐτήν,
τῇ νίσοντο φορῆες ὅτε τρυγόῳεν ἀλωήν.
sentences.l:
and one only path was to it,
by which the carriers went whenever they harvested the vineyard.
sentences.i: and there was only one path to it, by which the carriers went whenever they harvested the vineyard.
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 565. μία … οἴη ‘one only’; ἀταρπιτός ‘path’; ἦεν = ἦν ‘was’; ἐπ’ αὐτήν ‘to it’ (the vineyard). νίσοντο ‘went’ (νίσομαι); φορῆες ‘carriers’; ὅτε with the optative τρυγόῳεν ‘whenever they harvested’ (τρυγάω ‘gather in the crop’).

sentences.t:
παρθενικαὶ δὲ καὶ ἠΐθεοι ἀταλὰ φρονέοντες
πλεκτοῖς ἐν ταλάροισι φέρον μελιηδέα καρπόν.
sentences.l:
And maidens and young men, thinking tender thoughts,
in woven baskets carried the honey-sweet fruit.
sentences.i: Girls and young men, with tender thoughts in their hearts, carried the honey-sweet fruit in woven baskets.
sentences.n: παρθενική ‘maiden’; ἠΐθεος ‘unmarried young man’. ἀταλὰ φρονέοντες ‘thinking tender thoughts’: ἀταλός is ‘tender’ (as in ἀταλάφρων ‘tender-minded’), and the Greek does not say what the thoughts are. πλεκτός ‘woven’; τάλαρος ‘basket’; μελιηδής ‘honey-sweet’; καρπός ‘fruit’.

sentences.t:
τοῖσιν δ’ ἐν μέσσοισι πάϊς φόρμιγγι λιγείῃ
ἱμερόεν κιθάριζε, λίνον δ’ ὑπὸ καλὸν ἄειδε
λεπταλέῃ φωνῇ·
sentences.i: In the middle of them a boy played a clear-sounding lyre with a sound full of longing, and sang the song of Linos beautifully to it in a slender voice;
sentences.n: φόρμιγγι λιγείῃ ‘on a clear-sounding lyre’; κιθάριζε ‘played the lyre’, and ἱμερόεν (‘full of longing’) is used as an adverb. λίνον is uncertain: it is either the Linos-song, a dirge sung in harvest, or the linen string of the lyre (‘sang beautifully to the string’), and the word order allows both; the translation takes the song. ὑπό ‘beneath’ means to the lyre’s accompaniment. καλόν is taken as an adverb, ‘beautifully’. λεπταλέη ‘slender, thin’.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δὲ ῥήσσοντες ἁμαρτῇ
μολπῇ τ’ ἰυγμῷ τε ποσὶ σκαίροντες ἕποντο.
sentences.l:
and they, stamping together,
with song and dance and shouting, skipping with their feet, followed.
sentences.i: and the rest followed, stamping together, skipping on their feet with song and dance and whoops.
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 571. τοί is the article as a pronoun, ‘they’, the young dancers. ῥήσσοντες is literally ‘striking’, with the ground understood: stamping. ἁμαρτῇ ‘together, in step’. μολπή ‘song and dance’; ἰυγμός ‘whoop, shout’; σκαίρω ‘skip, bound’; ἕποντο ‘followed’ the boy.

sentences.t: ἐν δ’ ἀγέλην ποίησε βοῶν ὀρθοκραιράων·
sentences.l: And on it he made a herd of straight-horned cattle;
sentences.i: And on it he made a herd of straight-horned cattle;
sentences.n: ποίησε ‘made’ stands where ἐτίθει stood for the previous scenes. ἀγέλη ‘herd’. ὀρθοκραίρων (here ὀρθοκραιράων, with the long epic ending) ‘straight-horned’ is a compound of ὀρθός ‘straight’ and κραίρα, a form of κέρας ‘horn’; the Odyssey uses it of cattle too.

sentences.t:
αἳ δὲ βόες χρυσοῖο τετεύχατο κασσιτέρου τε,
μυκηθμῷ δ’ ἀπὸ κόπρου ἐπεσσεύοντο νομὸν δὲ
πὰρ ποταμὸν κελάδοντα, παρὰ ῥοδανὸν δονακῆα.
sentences.l:
and the cattle were made of gold and of tin,
and with lowing from the dung-yard they rushed to the pasture
beside a resounding river, beside the swaying reed-bed.
sentences.i: and the cattle were made of gold and tin; lowing, they hurried from the farmyard to the pasture beside a loud river, beside a swaying reed-bed.
sentences.n: τετεύχατο ‘were made’ (pluperfect passive of τεύχω). μυκηθμός ‘lowing’; κόπρος is dung, and ἀπὸ κόπρου means from the yard where the dung lies, the farmyard. ἐπεσσεύοντο ‘were hurrying’; νομὸν δέ ‘to the pasture’ (the suffix -δε gives direction). κελάδοντα ‘resounding’. ῥοδανὸν δονακῆα is a rare phrase whose exact sense is not certain: δόναξ is ‘reed’, ῥοδανός is taken as ‘swaying’, and the pair is read as a bed of waving reeds.

sentences.t:
χρύσειοι δὲ νομῆες ἅμ’ ἐστιχόωντο βόεσσι
τέσσαρες, ἐννέα δέ σφι κύνες πόδας ἀργοὶ ἕποντο.
sentences.l:
And golden herdsmen were marching along with the cattle,
four of them, and nine dogs, swift in foot, followed them.
sentences.i: Four golden herdsmen walked along with the cattle, and nine swift dogs followed them.
sentences.n: χρύσειοι νομῆες ‘golden herdsmen’ are figures of gold. ἐστιχόωντο ‘were marching in line’ (from στίχος ‘row’). σφι ‘them’ (the herdsmen). πόδας is an accusative of respect, ‘in feet’, with ἀργοί, which is either ‘swift’ or ‘white, gleaming’; the ancients disputed it, and ‘swift’ is used here, as for the dogs elsewhere.

sentences.t:
σμερδαλέω δὲ λέοντε δύ’ ἐν πρώτῃσι βόεσσι
ταῦρον ἐρύγμηλον ἐχέτην·
sentences.l:
And two frightful lions among the foremost cattle
a bellowing bull were holding;
sentences.i: But two frightful lions among the foremost cattle held a bellowing bull;
sentences.n: σμερδαλέω … λέοντε and ἐχέτην are duals: ‘the two frightful lions’, ‘the two held’; δύ’ repeats the number. σμερδαλέος ‘frightful’. ἐρύγμηλος ‘bellowing’, from ἐρεύγομαι ‘roar, belch’. The bull is at the head of the herd.

sentences.t:
ὃ δὲ μακρὰ μεμυκὼς
ἕλκετο· τὸν δὲ κύνες μετεκίαθον ἠδ’ αἰζηοί.
sentences.l:
and he, having bellowed long and loud,
was dragged; and after him went dogs and vigorous men.
sentences.i: and he, lowing long and loud, was dragged along; and the dogs and the vigorous men went after him.
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 580. ὃ δέ ‘and he’ is the bull. μακρά is adverbial, ‘long, loudly’, and μεμυκώς is the perfect participle of μυκάομαι ‘low, bellow’, with a present sense. ἕλκετο is passive, ‘was dragged’. μετεκίαθον ‘went after’, as at 532. αἰζηός ‘vigorous man, young man in his strength’.

sentences.t:
τὼ μὲν ἀναρρήξαντε βοὸς μεγάλοιο βοείην
ἔγκατα καὶ μέλαν αἷμα λαφύσσετον·
sentences.l:
The two, having torn up the hide of the great ox,
entrails and black blood were gulping down;
sentences.i: The two lions tore open the hide of the great ox and gulped down its entrails and black blood;
sentences.n: τώ is the dual article, ‘the two’ (the lions). ἀναρρήξαντε is the dual aorist participle of ἀναρρήγνυμι ‘tear open’. βοείη ‘oxhide’; ἔγκατα ‘entrails’; λαφύσσετον is dual, ‘the two gulp down’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ νομῆες
αὔτως ἐνδίεσαν ταχέας κύνας ὀτρύνοντες.
sentences.l:
and the herdsmen
just so were setting on the swift dogs, urging them.
sentences.i: while the herdsmen set the swift dogs on to no purpose, urging them forward.
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 583. αὔτως ‘just so’, that is, to no effect, as the next lines show. ἐνδίεσαν ‘were setting on’ is from the rare verb ἐνδίημι; ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἤτοι δακέειν μὲν ἀπετρωπῶντο λεόντων,
ἱστάμενοι δὲ μάλ’ ἐγγὺς ὑλάκτεον ἔκ τ’ ἀλέοντο.
sentences.l:
But these indeed from biting the lions were shrinking back,
and standing very near they barked and kept dodging out of the way.
sentences.i: But the dogs shrank from biting the lions; they stood very close and barked, and kept dodging out of the way.
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ‘but they’ are the dogs. ἤτοι is printed as one word in this edition. ἀπετρωπῶντο ‘were turning away from’ (ἀποτρωπάομαι) takes the infinitive δακέειν ‘from biting’ and the genitive λεόντων. ὑλάκτεον ‘barked’; ἔκ τ’ ἀλέοντο ‘and dodged out’ (ἐξαλέομαι).

sentences.t:
ἐν δὲ νομὸν ποίησε περικλυτὸς ἀμφιγυήεις
ἐν καλῇ βήσσῃ μέγαν οἰῶν ἀργεννάων,
σταθμούς τε κλισίας τε κατηρεφέας ἰδὲ σηκούς.
sentences.l:
And a pasture made the very-famous both-limbed one
in a fine glen, a great one, of white sheep,
steadings and huts roofed-over and pens.
sentences.i: And on it the very famous both-limbed god made a great pasture of white sheep in a fine glen, with steadings and roofed huts and pens.
sentences.n: The maker is Hephaestus, named by his epithet περικλυτὸς ἀμφιγυήεις, whose second word is not understood: ‘lame in both legs’ and ‘strong in both arms’ have been guessed. νομός ‘pasture’; βήσσα ‘glen’; ἀργεννός ‘white’. σταθμοί ‘steadings’ (farm-buildings), κλισίαι ‘huts’, κατηρεφής ‘roofed over’, σηκός ‘pen’; the three are listed with τε … τε … ἰδέ.

sentences.t:
ἐν δὲ χορὸν ποίκιλλε περικλυτὸς ἀμφιγυήεις,
τῷ ἴκελον οἷόν ποτ’ ἐνὶ Κνωσῷ εὐρείῃ
Δαίδαλος ἤσκησεν καλλιπλοκάμῳ Ἀριάδνῃ.
sentences.l:
And a dancing-ground he wrought intricately, the very-famous both-limbed one,
like that which once in broad Knossos
Daedalus made for fair-plaited Ariadne.
sentences.i: And the very famous both-limbed god worked an intricate dancing-ground, like the one that Daedalus once made in broad Knossos for fair-plaited Ariadne.
sentences.n: ποίκιλλε ‘worked intricately’ (ποικίλλω). χορός is the dancing-ground and the dance held on it, and the next lines show dancers on it. τῷ ἴκελον οἷον ‘like that which’; ἤσκησεν ‘fashioned with skill’ (ἀσκέω). Δαίδαλος is the legendary craftsman, Κνωσός is Knossos in Crete, and the Greek tells nothing more of Ariadne than the epithet καλλιπλόκαμος ‘fair-plaited’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα μὲν ἠΐθεοι καὶ παρθένοι ἀλφεσίβοιαι
ὀρχεῦντ’ ἀλλήλων ἐπὶ καρπῷ χεῖρας ἔχοντες.
sentences.l:
There young men and ox-earning maidens
were dancing, holding hands at one another’s wrist.
sentences.i: There young men and maidens who bring their families oxen were dancing, holding one another by the wrist.
sentences.n: ἀλφεσίβοιαι is ‘earning oxen’ (ἀλφάνω ‘earn, fetch’ + βοῦς), the usual explanation being that suitors paid in oxen for a girl, so that a maiden brings her father oxen; the sense is not quite certain. ὀρχεῦντ’ = ὠρχεῦντο ‘were dancing’, unaugmented. ἀλλήλων ἐπὶ καρπῷ ‘at one another’s wrist’; καρπός here is ‘wrist’, not ‘fruit’.

sentences.t:
τῶν δ’ αἳ μὲν λεπτὰς ὀθόνας ἔχον, οἳ δὲ χιτῶνας
εἵατ’ ἐϋννήτους, ἦκα στίλβοντας ἐλαίῳ·
sentences.l:
Of these the girls wore fine linen cloths, and the young men
were dressed in well-spun tunics, faintly shining with oil;
sentences.i: Of these the girls wore fine linen robes, and the young men were dressed in well-spun tunics, faintly glistening with oil;
sentences.n: τῶν δ’ ‘of these’ divides the dancers: αἳ μέν ‘the girls’, οἳ δέ ‘the young men’. ὀθόνη is a fine linen cloth worn as a garment. εἵατο ‘were dressed in’ is from ἕννυμι, not ἧμαι ‘sit’ (the same form serves for both). ἐϋννήτους ‘well-spun’; ἦκα ‘faintly, softly’; στίλβοντας ‘glistening’; ἐλαίῳ ‘with oil’.

sentences.t:
καί ῥ’ αἳ μὲν καλὰς στεφάνας ἔχον, οἳ δὲ μαχαίρας
εἶχον χρυσείας ἐξ ἀργυρέων τελαμώνων.
sentences.l:
and the girls had fine garlands, and the young men
had knives of gold from silver straps.
sentences.i: and the girls wore fine garlands, and the young men carried golden knives from silver straps.
sentences.n: καί ῥ’ = καὶ ῥα. στεφάνη here is a garland for the head. μάχαιρα is a large knife, not a sword. τελαμών ‘strap’ is the strap that carries the knife. ἔχον and εἶχον are both imperfects of ἔχω, ‘wore, had’; ἐξ ‘from’ the straps they hang.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ὁτὲ μὲν θρέξασκον ἐπισταμένοισι πόδεσσι
ῥεῖα μάλ’, ὡς ὅτε τις τροχὸν ἄρμενον ἐν παλάμῃσιν
ἑζόμενος κεραμεὺς πειρήσεται, αἴ κε θέῃσιν·
sentences.i: At one time they would run on skilful feet, very easily, as when a potter sits and tries a wheel fitted to his hands, to see whether it will run;
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ‘these’ are the dancers. θρέξασκον is the iterative aorist of τρέχω, ‘would run’. ἐπισταμένοισι πόδεσσι ‘with knowing feet’, that is, skilfully (ἐπίσταμαι ‘know how’); ῥεῖα μάλα ‘very easily’. ὡς ὅτε τις … πειρήσεται is a simile, with πειρήσεται ‘tries’ (a short-vowel subjunctive or a future); αἴ κε θέῃσιν ‘whether it will run’ (θέω), meaning that the wheel spins freely. τροχός ‘wheel’; ἄρμενον ‘fitted’; παλάμη ‘palm’; κεραμεύς ‘potter’.

sentences.t: ἄλλοτε δ’ αὖ θρέξασκον ἐπὶ στίχας ἀλλήλοισι.
sentences.l: and at another time again they would run in rows toward one another.
sentences.i: and at another time again they would run in lines to meet one another.
sentences.n: ὁτὲ μέν … ἄλλοτε δ’ αὖ ‘at one time … at another again’ balances the two movements, and θρέξασκον is the iterative again. ἐπὶ στίχας ‘into rows’; ἀλλήλοισι ‘toward one another’ (dative).

sentences.t:
πολλὸς δ’ ἱμερόεντα χορὸν περιίσταθ’ ὅμιλος
τερπόμενοι·
sentences.l:
And a great throng stood around the dancing-ground full of longing,
delighting;
sentences.i: A great throng stood around the dancing-ground, which was full of longing, in delight;
sentences.n: περιίσταθ’ = περιίστατο ‘stood around’ (middle imperfect, singular to agree with ὅμιλος; the final τ becomes θ before the rough breathing of ὅμιλος). ὅμιλος ‘throng’ is singular but τερπόμενοι ‘delighting’ is plural, since many are meant. ἱμερόεις ‘full of longing’ (ἵμερος ‘longing’), the dancing-ground that stirs the watchers. This unit begins at 603 and ends in the middle of 604.

sentences.t:
μετὰ δέ σφιν ἐμέλπετο θεῖος ἀοιδὸς
φορμίζων·
sentences.l:
and among them was celebrating a divine minstrel,
playing the lyre;
sentences.i: and among them a divine minstrel made music, playing the lyre;
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 604. μετά … σφιν ‘among them’. ἐμέλπετο is the imperfect of μέλπομαι ‘celebrate with song and dance’, which here means taking part in the music. θεῖος ‘divine’, as the Odyssey has it of a minstrel. φορμίζων is the participle of φορμίζω ‘play the φόρμιγξ, the lyre’.

sentences.t:
δοιὼ δὲ κυβιστητῆρε κατ’ αὐτοὺς
μολπῆς ἐξάρχοντες ἐδίνευον κατὰ μέσσους.
sentences.l:
and two tumblers among them,
leading off the song and dance, were whirling through the midst.
sentences.i: and two tumblers among them led off the song and dance, whirling through the middle.
sentences.n: This unit begins in the middle of line 605. δοιώ … κυβιστητῆρε is a dual, ‘two tumblers’ (κυβιστάω ‘tumble head over heels’), though the participle ἐξάρχοντες is plural. κατ’ αὐτούς ‘among them’, the dancers. μολπῆς ἐξάρχοντες ‘leading off the song and dance’ (genitive after ἐξάρχω); ἐδίνευον ‘were whirling’, like ἐδίνεον at 494.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ ἐτίθει ποταμοῖο μέγα σθένος Ὠκεανοῖο
ἄντυγα πὰρ πυμάτην σάκεος πύκα ποιητοῖο.
sentences.l:
And on it he set the great strength of the river Oceanus
along the outermost rim of the well-wrought shield.
sentences.i: And on it he set the great strength of the river Oceanus, along the outermost rim of the well-made shield.
sentences.n: Ὠκεανός is the river that encircles the world, so it runs round the shield’s edge, and σθένος ‘strength’ means the great flow of it. ἄντυξ is the rim (as at 479), and πυμάτην ‘last, outermost’. πύκα ποιητοῖο ‘well, closely wrought’ (πύκα ‘closely, firmly’; ποιητός ‘made’).

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δὴ τεῦξε σάκος μέγα τε στιβαρόν τε,
τεῦξ’ ἄρα οἱ θώρηκα φαεινότερον πυρὸς αὐγῆς,
sentences.l:
But when he had made the shield, great and stout,
then he made for him a breastplate brighter than the gleam of fire,
sentences.i: When he had made the shield, great and stout, he made for him a breastplate brighter than the gleam of fire,
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐπεί begins the list of the rest of the armour. τεῦξε, aorist of τεύχω ‘make’, opens each clause (610, 611, 613). οἱ ‘for him’ is Achilles. θώρηξ ‘breastplate’ is here the accusative θώρηκα. φαεινότερον is the comparative of φαεινός ‘shining’, with the genitive πυρὸς αὐγῆς ‘than the gleam of fire’.

sentences.t:
τεῦξε δέ οἱ κόρυθα βριαρὴν κροτάφοις ἀραρυῖαν
καλὴν δαιδαλέην, ἐπὶ δὲ χρύσεον λόφον ἧκε,
sentences.l:
and he made for him a helmet, heavy, fitted to the temples,
fine, cunningly wrought, and on it set a golden crest,
sentences.i: and he made for him a heavy helmet, fitted to his temples, fine and cunningly wrought, and set a golden crest on it,
sentences.n: κόρυς ‘helmet’, accusative κόρυθα. βριαρή ‘heavy’. κροτάφοις ἀραρυῖαν ‘fitted to the temples’ (ἀραρυῖα, perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω ‘fit’). δαιδαλέη ‘cunningly wrought’. ἐπὶ … ἧκε ‘set on it’ (ἵημι ‘send, put’); λόφος ‘crest’.

sentences.t: τεῦξε δέ οἱ κνημῖδας ἑανοῦ κασσιτέροιο.
sentences.l: and he made for him greaves of pliant tin.
sentences.i: and he made for him greaves of pliant tin.
sentences.n: κνημῖδες ‘greaves’ are shin-guards, as in ἐϋκνήμιδες ‘well-greaved’. ἑανός is an adjective here, taken as ‘pliant’ (ancient glosses also give ‘fine’); its sense is not certain. κασσίτερος ‘tin’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ πάνθ’ ὅπλα κάμε κλυτὸς ἀμφιγυήεις,
μητρὸς Ἀχιλλῆος θῆκε προπάροιθεν ἀείρας.
sentences.l:
But when he had toiled to make all the arms, the famous both-limbed one,
before the mother of Achilles he laid them, having lifted them up.
sentences.i: And when the famous both-limbed god had toiled to finish all the armour, he lifted it up and laid it down before the mother of Achilles.
sentences.n: κλυτός ‘famous’ is the shorter form of the epithet used at 587 and 590 (‘very famous’). κάμε ‘toiled to make’ (aorist of κάμνω). ὅπλα ‘arms’ here means the armour he has just made. μητρὸς Ἀχιλλῆος is Thetis, who is not named but is the one he was making it for. θῆκε ‘laid’; προπάροιθεν ‘before, in front of’; ἀείρας ‘having lifted’.

sentences.t:
ἣ δ’ ἴρηξ ὣς ἆλτο κατ’ Οὐλύμπου νιφόεντος
τεύχεα μαρμαίροντα παρ’ Ἡφαίστοιο φέρουσα.
sentences.l:
And she like a hawk sprang down from snowy Olympus,
bearing the sparkling armour from Hephaestus.
sentences.i: And she sprang like a hawk down from snowy Olympus, carrying the sparkling armour from Hephaestus.
sentences.n: ἣ δ’ is Thetis. ἴρηξ ὥς ‘like a hawk’, with the noun placed before ὥς. ἆλτο is the aorist of ἅλλομαι ‘leap’; κατ’ Οὐλύμπου ‘down from Olympus’ (κατά with the genitive); νιφόεις ‘snowy’. τεύχεα μαρμαίροντα ‘the sparkling armour’; παρ’ Ἡφαίστοιο ‘from Hephaestus’ (παρά with the genitive of the one who gives). The book ends here.
